newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: INTERVIEW - Alcatel expects more ADSL contracts soon.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Alcatel expects more ADSL contracts soon.

text.p: French telecoms equipment group Alcatel Alsthom expects to announce at least two big contracts to supply ADSL technology over the next month, a senior company official said on Tuesday.
The ADSL (Asymmetric Digital Subscriber Line) technology enables high-speed access to the Internet and other networks through existing telephone copper-wiring infrastructure.

"We are expecting to announce some important contracts very soon, within one month. We expect at least two big contracts and then a number of smaller ones to follow," said Martin De Prycker, Alcatel's vice president for the access systems division.

De Prycker, in Singapore for the Asia Telecom 97 trade fair, told Reuters in an interview the contracts were likely to come from both Europe and Asia but declined to reveal the size of the deals or say who were the parties involved.
De Prycker said ADSL technology should take off in a big way in 1999-2000 after trials are conducted in 1996-1997.
By that time, Alcatel expects revenue from ADSL to reach almost one billion French francs (US$172 million).
"We are expecting something like 150 million French francs this year and to grow and more than triple in the coming year," "We are expecting close to one billion French francs by year 2000," he said.
In Singapore, Singapore Telecommunications Ltd (SingTel) has already deployed 1,200 ADSL lines and Alcatel is hoping another 10,000 lines would be added by the end of 1997, De Prycker said.
De Prycker told a news conference that Alcatel saw some 50,000-100,000 ADSL lines being tested and deployed this year.
"We expect the real market takeoff in 1999-2000," he said.
The market potential was as big as 600 million lines based on the same number of existing telephone lines already installed, he said.
Internet usage, expected to rise to more than 200 million subscribers in 2000, would drive the market for ADSL through the need for greater bandwidth, he said.
The advantage of ADSL was not only faster speed in accessing all kinds of different data on networks but that the telephone could be used at the same time.
The user can also have a permanent connection to the network yet pay only for the data transported.
Alcatel is in discussions with various companies to license its ADSL technology, De Prycker said.
